title: Hypocalcaemia after thyroidectomy
subtitle: Predict with PTH, treat symptoms with IV calcium

sources.title: American Thyroid Association statement on postoperative hypoparathyroidism: diagnosis, prevention, and management in adults (Orloff LA et al., Thyroid)
Society for Endocrinology Endocrine Emergency Guidance: emergency management of acute hypocalcaemia in adult patients (Turner J, Gittoes N, Selby P, Endocr Connect)
European Society of Endocrinology Clinical Guideline: treatment of chronic hypoparathyroidism in adults (Bollerslev J et al., Eur J Endocrinol)

red_flags.text: Carpopedal spasm, tetany, seizures, laryngospasm or bronchospasm: severe acute hypocalcaemia.
Adjusted calcium below 1.9 mmol/L, even without symptoms.
Perioral tingling or paraesthesia of the fingers in the first days after total or completion thyroidectomy or central neck dissection.

do_now.text: Severe symptoms or adjusted calcium below 1.9 mmol/L: 10 to 20 mL of 10% calcium gluconate in 50 to 100 mL of 5% glucose IV over 10 minutes, with ECG monitoring.
Follow the bolus with a calcium gluconate infusion per the Society for Endocrinology regimen, titrated to calcium checked frequently at first.
Check and correct magnesium: hypocalcaemia does not correct while magnesium is low.
Mild symptoms or a modest fall: oral calcium, with active vitamin D (calcitriol or alfacalcidol) when PTH is low.

assess.text: Ask specifically about tingling around the mouth and in the fingers; examine for Chvostek and Trousseau signs.
Adjusted calcium, phosphate, magnesium and PTH.
Operative note: how many parathyroids were seen, whether any were autotransplanted, and whether a central neck dissection was done.

investigate.text: Post-operative PTH within hours of surgery predicts hypocalcaemia and guides early supplementation. Thresholds depend on the assay and units used locally.
Serial adjusted calcium: the nadir commonly falls on the first or second day after surgery.
Vitamin D level, ideally checked before surgery so deficiency can be corrected in advance.

resuscitate.text: Do not give IV calcium through a small peripheral vein if avoidable: extravasation causes tissue necrosis. Use a large vein and dilute as per protocol.
Avoid mixing calcium with bicarbonate or phosphate-containing solutions.

definitive.text: Low post-operative PTH: start oral calcium and active vitamin D early, before symptoms, per local protocol, and wean as parathyroid function recovers.
Discharge with written advice about symptoms, a calcium check within days, and a clear weaning plan.
Persisting hypoparathyroidism needs endocrine follow-up, aiming for low-normal calcium without symptoms and avoiding hypercalciuria.

escalate.text: Senior review and cardiac monitoring for tetany, seizures, laryngospasm, arrhythmia or calcium below 1.9 mmol/L.
Endocrinology for refractory hypocalcaemia or for hypoparathyroidism that persists beyond the early weeks.
Feed back hypoparathyroidism rates to the surgeon: it is an audited outcome of thyroid surgery.

notes: Hypocalcaemia is a parathyroid problem created at operation. Seeing and preserving the glands on their blood supply prevents most of it.
Most early post-thyroidectomy hypoparathyroidism is temporary; plan the weaning, or patients stay on calcitriol for years unnecessarily.
Magnesium is the forgotten electrolyte. Check it in every patient who does not respond to calcium.
